FICTIONAL TEST ESSAY, written by ChatGPT on request (November 2026). Not a real applicant.

At 12:17 on a Tuesday afternoon, my program announced that every student in our peer tutoring
club had been assigned a tutor. I was pretty proud of it. Then our club coordinator pointed out
that three students had no one to meet, two tutors had been assigned to the same room, and
one student had been matched with someone who wasn't even available that day.

I stared at the screen for a few seconds. The program had worked exactly as I had written it.
Unfortunately, I had written it badly.

I had volunteered to build a small Python program to help organize our school's peer tutoring
club. Until then, the coordinator had been managing everything through spreadsheets,
messages, and a remarkable ability to remember everyone's schedules. I thought the solution
was straightforward: collect everyone's subjects and availability, compare the information, and
find the best matches.

It sounded like a problem made for a computer.

For the first few days, I enjoyed the process more than I expected. I liked breaking a messy task
into smaller pieces. I liked watching a few lines of code turn into something useful. When I finally
got the matching algorithm to run without errors, I sent the results to the coordinator almost
immediately.

That was when I discovered how little I had considered the people using it.

Some students had written their availability in ways my program couldn't understand. Others
had selected every available time because they didn't know which sessions would be
comfortable for them. One student had a specific reason for requesting a particular tutor, but my
form had never given them a place to explain it.

I had reduced everyone's situation to a few columns in a spreadsheet.

I initially wanted to fix everything by adding more conditions to the code. But after talking to the
coordinator, I realized that the bigger problem was the way I had collected the information. I had
designed the system around what was convenient for me to program, not what was convenient
for the people using it.

So I went back to the beginning. I changed the form, added an optional section for special
requests, and made the program suggest possible matches instead of making the final decision.
The coordinator could review the suggestions and speak with students before confirming
anything.
It wasn't an especially impressive piece of software. It didn't use machine learning or some
complicated algorithm. In fact, the final version was probably less technically ambitious than my
first attempt.

But it was more useful.

That experience changed the way I think about computer science. I used to see programming
primarily as a process of finding the right instructions to give a machine. Now I see it as a
process that begins long before the first line of code. It begins with deciding what problem is
worth solving, asking the right questions, and understanding the people affected by the solution.

I still enjoy spending an unreasonable amount of time debugging a program. There is something
satisfying about finding the one small mistake responsible for a much bigger problem. But I have
also learned that not every problem can be solved by looking at the code.

I want to study computer science because I enjoy the combination of logic, creativity, and
uncertainty it brings. I am particularly interested in how computing, data, and artificial
intelligence can help people make better decisions. At Harvard, I hope to explore these areas
while learning from people who approach problems differently from me. I don't expect to arrive
with all the answers. Honestly, I would rather be surrounded by people who make me realize
how many questions I haven't thought to ask.

I still have the original version of that tutoring program saved on my laptop. Sometimes I open it
and look at the code. It reminds me of how excited I was when it first ran successfully.

It also reminds me that a program can be technically correct and still get the problem completely
wrong.
